newsitem.title: USA: CIS, East Europe lead deficit to continue - Noranda.
newsitem.headline: CIS, East Europe lead deficit to continue - Noranda.

text.p: The Commonwealth of Independent States and Eastern Europe will continue to be short of lead for some time to come but mine output has started to climb gradually, albeit from a low level, Tom Schnull, manager of lead sales at Canada's Noranda Mining and Exploration Inc said.

"We expect that the CIS and Eastern Europe will remain net importers of concentrates as smelter production outpaces mined production," Schnull told the U.S. Lead Industries Association annual meeting.

CIS lead mining output has fallen each year since 1988 because few could operate successfully in a free market economy, Schnull said. Mines were also suffering from low ore grades and lack of money, but smelters with huge spare capacity will slowly suck in surplus Western concentrates in coming years.
Schnull forecast that the CIS and Eastern Europe end 1997 with a mined lead in concentrates deficit of 20,000 tonnes, compared with 24,000 tonnes in 1996.
The forecast includes 29,000 tonnes of lead in concentrates exports to the West, and imports of 48,000 tonnes, compared with 30,000 tonnes and 43,000 tonnes respectively last year.

Schnull estimated that CIS and Eastern Europe mine production will rise eight percent this year to 184,000 tonnes of lead in concentrates, reversing the declines of recent years. Avaliable mine production in the region was pegged at 203,000 tonnes, with smelter consumption at 223,000 tonnes.
This year the region was forecast to produce 217,000 tonnes of primary lead and 97,000 tonnes of secondary lead, bringing the total to 314,000 tonnes, up from last year's 299,000 tonnes.

Exports, net of imports, of refined metal from the CIS and Eastern Europe to the West this year will reach 38,000 tonnes, barely changed from last year, but expected to rise slightly as smelter output recovers more quickly than internal demand.

Demand for lead in Eastern Europe this year was put at 135,000 tonnes, up from 123,000 tonnes in 1996, while the CIS, which includes Russia, was expected to consume 154,000 tonnes compared with 146,000 tonnes last year.
Schnull expected the year to end with a 13,000 tonne deficit of refined metal in Eastern Europe and the CIS, compared with a 9,000 tonne shortfall last year.

Cash premiums on physical lead in Russia have soared to over $200 per tonne (over LME cash) due to high credit risk, lack of internal supply, and cash shortages among domestic consumers which put a dampener on imports, Schnull said.
"For the time being we can expect to see premiums stay at today's elevated levels," Schnull said.
